Class teacher's note, Class 9B, after the house captain election

Akash is one of the most liked students in this class. For the two weeks of the campaign, he told me more than once, "Ma'am, everyone's my friend, it's sorted." I did not see him make a poster or visit any class except ours.

His rival, Neelam, visited all eleven sections with a one-page list: a lost-and-found box, fixed fans in the Class 6 rooms, and a monthly house quiz. Juniors stopped me in the corridor to ask about her quiz.

Akash lost by forty votes. At dispersal he sat on the bench long after the others had left, turning his badge over and over.

I sat beside him and asked what he had learned. He said, "Being liked isn't a plan." I have asked him to help Neelam run the house quiz.

qa.a: Neelam visited all eleven sections with a one-page list.

qa.a: He was probably stunned and disappointed, perhaps a little ashamed, having been so sure his popularity would win.

qa.q: What approach could Akash have used instead of relying on being liked?
qa.a: He could have visited other classes and offered two or three concrete ideas, since juniors were clearly drawn to specific proposals like the quiz.

qa.q: How might the juniors in other sections have seen the two candidates?
qa.a: To them Neelam was a real person with a plan who came to their room, while Akash was mostly a name they had not heard from.

Thursday night

I lost. To Aditi. By a lot.

I keep replaying it. Last month I honestly thought the election was a formality. Half the school says hi to me in the corridor. The cricket team, the drama lot, my whole tuition batch. I didn't make a single poster because what's the point, everyone knows me.

Aditi went to every class with a sheet about the broken drinking taps and a plan for a book swap. She even talked to the Class 6 kids nobody bothers with.

Today in the hall I heard juniors say, "Aditi came to our class, she explained everything." Nobody said my name like that.

It stings. People like me, but they didn't know what I'd actually do. I'm Raghav, the guy with lots of friends and no plan. Next year I'm writing things down.

Nitin had one evening to prepare his two-minute speech for the class representative election, and the flat was chaos: his cousin's wedding was two days away, and the living room was full of aunties folding saris.

He took his draft to the only quiet place, the building's stairwell. First read-through: three minutes forty. Far too long.

He cut the list of five promises down to one: a proper notice board where every class's test dates were posted. Then he kept one story, about missing a chemistry test because the date changed and nobody told him.

His friend Simran came down with two cups of tea. "Go again. I'll time you." He practised facing the stairwell window like a mirror. Two minutes ten.

"Cut 'basically'," Simran said. "You said it six times." Next run: one minute fifty-five.

Chandrika's speech for school vice-captain began as two full pages. On Sunday afternoon, in the small bedroom of their Chembur flat, she read it aloud to the wardrobe mirror with her phone timer running. Five minutes. The limit was two.

She crossed out every sentence that began with "Also". What remained was one promise: a student helpdesk at the gate every Monday. And one story: the morning a new girl had cried near the gate because she couldn't find her classroom.

Her younger brother Omkar was dragged in as the audience. "Say it without looking," he said. She tried. She forgot the second half.

They ran it four more times. Omkar pointed out she said "like" constantly, so she cut it. By evening she could do it in one minute fifty, looking at him the whole time.

"If I'm school captain," she shouted, "no homework on weekends! And two free trips every year!"

The hall roared. Her friends banged the benches. Nikita, standing at the back, didn't clap.

Wei sat in the library of his school in Vancouver with the old student newsletter archive open. He wanted to be student council president, and he had one question: why had Maya Okafor won so easily two years ago?

He read her campaign flyers, then the newsletters from her term. There were no big speeches. In her first month she got the broken water fountains on the second floor fixed. In her second, she added a bike rack. Small things, but people saw them every day.

"So trust came from visible fixes," Wei muttered.

His friend Santiago leaned over. "Fountains are fixed now, though."

"Right. So what's broken now?" They walked the halls and found it: the lockers near the gym jammed constantly. Wei's poster the next week said: "Working lockers by November. Then the next thing."

qa.a: The lockers near the gym jammed constantly.

qa.a: It suggests he felt a spark of excitement and confidence, having found a pattern he could use rather than copying her exact promises.

qa.q: What would be a risk if Wei had copied Maya's promises exactly?
qa.a: He would promise to fix fountains that already work, which would look out of touch; adapting the idea of small visible fixes to current problems avoids that.

qa.a: Santiago probably feels convinced and involved, since his remark about the fixed fountains pushed Wei to look for what is broken now.

Urmila, you're worried about the student union election at your college? Let me tell you about your Binita pishi at sixteen, in our school in Kolkata.

My rival was Mitali. We had been best friends till Class 8, then drifted. During the campaign, some of my supporters found out she had failed a maths test. "Put it on a poster," they said.

I went home and sat on this very verandah. I thought: if I shame her, I am telling everyone that's how a captain behaves. And Mitali and I have walked to the tram together for years.

I lost. But Mitali invited me to her wedding twenty years later, and I stood beside her. Some losses are small.

Tuesday, after assembly

Writing this in the library because my hands are still a bit shaky, but in a good way.

Last night I nearly dropped out of the election. I kept imagining standing in front of 600 people and my mind going blank, like it did in the Class 7 elocution.

So this morning I did what Disha showed me. In the washroom before assembly: breathe in for four counts, out for six, five times. My heart was still fast but not galloping. I wrote three points on a small card: water filters, a cycle shed, a monthly open meeting. Just three words each.

On stage I found Disha in the third row and talked to her like it was just us. I looked at the card once. I finished all three points.

I'm Rafiq, and I didn't freeze. That feels huge.

Last September I lost the school captain election to Parul by six votes. Six. I remember standing near the notice board, face burning, pretending to read a sports fixture.

I wanted to disappear for a week. Instead, before lunch, I walked to Parul's class and shook her hand. She looked surprised, then said, "Thanks. Your canteen idea was good, you know."

Then I went to Parul again and offered to run a canteen committee under her. She agreed. Now four of us meet every Friday, and last month the canteen finally started a second billing counter.

I'm Jatin. I'm not captain, but the thing I campaigned for happened anyway.

Our model of a village bridge is finally on track, and I think I cracked why the last one wasn't.

Last time we all started with the fun bits. Someone painted, someone wired the lights, and then we found the painted parts had to be sanded off to glue the frame. Wasted a week.

This time I sat down on Sunday and asked: what has to wait for what? The frame needs two days to dry. Painting can't start till then. The LED lights can't be tested till the circuit works. But the poster and the written report don't need anything.

So on Monday, the very first thing, Faisal and I glued the frame. Rhea started the circuit the same day. Meanwhile Om wrote the report. By Thursday the frame was dry and painting began.

Nothing is waiting anymore. It feels almost too easy.

Love,
Nikita

passage:
People think I was just bossy, Vinita, but no, there was a reason. Let me tell it properly.

I'm Irawati. Our Class 10 group had to build a working model of a water pump for the district exhibition in three weeks. Everyone wanted to start with the painting, because that's the fun part.

I drew the steps on a paper plate in the canteen. The wooden base had to be glued and left to set before anything went on it. The pump couldn't be tested until the motor circuit worked. The chart and the explanation card didn't depend on anything.

So I said: base and circuit start today, first. Chart people, start whenever. Painting waits.

Two of the girls sulked. But on day nine, the base was solid, the circuit ran, and we tested water flow. The group that started with paint was still waiting for glue at the exhibition.

qa.a: Irawati drew the steps on a paper plate in the canteen.

qa.q: How did two of the girls feel when painting had to wait?
qa.a: They felt annoyed and sulky, because painting was the fun part and they had to hold off.

qa.q: What could Irawati say to make the order feel less bossy?
qa.a: Irawati could show the group the paper plate and explain the chain, so they see why painting waits instead of just being told.

qa.q: How might the girls who sulked see the plan by the exhibition?
qa.a: They would likely feel grateful and a bit sheepish, seeing their model tested while another group was still waiting for glue.
